_about: Health indicators for the astronaut self-assessment tool. Each indicator has (a) absolute clinical tiers from public Earth guidelines and (b) personal-baseline deviation tiers, because spaceflight shifts 'normal' (e.g. resting core temp ~+1 C, BP ~-8-10 mmHg). Triage rule of thumb: final tier = worst of absolute tier and deviation tier. Thresholds are hackathon/demo values, not NASA medical standards.

_tiers.red: Act - escalate to crew medical officer / flight surgeon

indicators.name: Resting heart rate
indicators.plain_meaning: How many times your heart beats per minute while resting.
indicators.how_to_measure: Chest strap / wrist monitor or 60 s manual pulse count, seated/still, before breakfast.
indicators.spaceflight_note: Shuttle-era 24 h studies found in-flight heart rate and its variability were reduced; long-duration ISS data show minimal change. A sustained rise from baseline can point to dehydration, infection, fever or stress.

red: Notify crew medical officer and flight surgeon

indicators.name: Blood pressure (systolic)
indicators.plain_meaning: The top number: pressure in your arteries when the heart beats.
indicators.how_to_measure: Automatic arm cuff, seated/restrained, arm at heart level, average 2 readings 1 min apart.
indicators.spaceflight_note: On the ISS, 24 h ambulatory BP falls by about 8-10 mmHg because blood vessels relax (systemic vascular resistance drops ~39%). So a reading that looks 'normal' on Earth may already be a rise from this astronaut's in-flight baseline.

red: If >180 systolic or with headache/vision change: notify flight surgeon now

indicators.name: Blood pressure (diastolic)
indicators.plain_meaning: The bottom number: pressure in your arteries between beats.
indicators.spaceflight_note: Diastolic pressure was reported lower in flight (about 5 mmHg in the first 2 weeks of Shuttle flights).

indicators.name: Blood glucose (fasting)
indicators.plain_meaning: Sugar level in your blood before eating - your body's main fuel.
indicators.how_to_measure: Finger-prick glucometer or continuous glucose monitor, before breakfast.
indicators.spaceflight_note: Spaceflight is associated with insulin-resistance signals (gene/pathway changes in astronauts; NASA Twins Study protein changes). Track upward drift.

amber: If low: 15-15 rule - eat 15 g fast carbs, re-check in 15 min
If high: review meal timing, re-test tomorrow
red: If <54: treat immediately with fast carbs, buddy check, notify crew medical officer
If >=126 repeatedly: flag to flight surgeon

indicators.name: Core body temperature
indicators.plain_meaning: The temperature inside your body. Too high can mean infection or overheating.
indicators.how_to_measure: Forehead heat-flux sensor (as used on ISS) or thermometer, at rest, same time daily.
indicators.spaceflight_note: IMPORTANT: on the ISS resting core temperature rises gradually over ~2.5 months to about 38 C (~1 C above Earth) and can exceed 40 C during exercise. A fixed 38 C fever cut-off would false-alarm constantly - use deviation from the astronaut's own in-flight baseline.

amber: Re-measure at rest in 30 min (not after exercise)
Check for symptoms: chills, sore throat, rash
red: Symptom checklist + notify crew medical officer

indicators.name: Blood oxygen saturation
indicators.plain_meaning: How much of your blood is carrying oxygen.
indicators.spaceflight_note: Not a classic spaceflight hazard, but relevant to the hostile closed environment (cabin CO2/air quality, EVA prep). Thresholds are general clinical convention - verify.
sources: general clinical convention - verify against challenge resources

indicators.name: Sleep duration
indicators.plain_meaning: How long you actually slept last night.
indicators.how_to_measure: Wrist actigraphy or self-report on waking.
indicators.spaceflight_note: NASA schedules 8.5 h, but a 10-year actigraphy study found ISS crews averaged just over 6 h; a newer NASA Ames analysis with more regular schedules found longer in-flight sleep. Sleep <5 h was linked to worse behavioural states. A single short night is only amber; the 3-day rolling average (amber <6 h, red <5 h) catches real sleep debt.

amber: Avoid caffeine late in the day
red: Talk to crew medical officer about sleep plan

indicators.name: Mood
indicators.plain_meaning: How you feel today: 1 = very low, 5 = great.
indicators.how_to_measure: Self-rating slider at end of day.
indicators.spaceflight_note: Isolation and confinement are one of NASA HRP's five hazards. Look for sustained dips, not one bad day.

red: Private conference with flight surgeon / behavioural health team

sources: NASA Human Research Program - five hazards of human spaceflight (see challenge Resources tab)

indicators.name: Stress
indicators.plain_meaning: How stressed you feel: 1 = calm, 5 = overwhelmed.
indicators.how_to_measure: Self-rating slider at end of day.
indicators.spaceflight_note: Spaceflight raises stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline), which suppress the immune system and are linked to latent virus reactivation.

indicators.name: Body mass
indicators.plain_meaning: Your body weight. In space this is measured by mass devices, not scales.
indicators.spaceflight_note: Decreased body mass is a documented spaceflight change (Twins Study); poor appetite is common. Loss also hints at muscle wasting / under-eating.

red: Nutrition plan review with flight surgeon

indicators.name: Exercise completed
indicators.plain_meaning: Minutes of prescribed exercise done today - your main defence against bone and muscle loss.
indicators.how_to_measure: Logged automatically from treadmill/cycle/resistance device or entered manually.
indicators.spaceflight_note: ISS crews exercise 1-2 h/day; calf muscle volume still fell ~13% over 6 months. Higher intensity protects muscle better than more volume.

red: Discuss schedule conflict with commander - bone/muscle loss accelerates

indicators.name: Eye check (Amsler grid)
indicators.plain_meaning: Weekly Amsler grid test. 0 = all lines straight, 1 = some lines wavy or blurred, 2 = a patch is missing or dark.
indicators.how_to_measure: Cover one eye, wear your usual reading correction, stare at the centre dot of the Amsler grid. Repeat with the other eye.
indicators.spaceflight_note: SANS (spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome): at least one feature found in 81% of NASA astronauts after long missions. Caused by head-ward fluid shift.

indicators.name: Mood check (PHQ-9)
indicators.plain_meaning: A validated 9-question screen for low mood over the last 2 weeks.
indicators.how_to_measure: Answer 9 quick questions in the check-in every 2 weeks.
indicators.spaceflight_note: PHQ-9 total of 10 or more is the standard screening cut-point (88% sensitivity and specificity for major depression in primary care). Validated on the general population, not astronauts; NASA uses its own behavioural suite (APEX) on missions. The last question (thoughts of self-harm) always triggers an urgent prompt.

amber: Keep routines: exercise, sleep, private calls home
red: Book a private conference with the behavioural health team or flight surgeon today

_range_convention: All tier ranges are half-open [lo, hi). Lookup order: if value falls in any red range -> red; elif any amber range -> amber; else green.
_baseline_method: Personal baseline = median of the astronaut's GREEN readings from 7 to 21 days ago. Lagged so a slow drift over 1-2 weeks isn't absorbed into 'normal'; green-only so a flagged episode doesn't become the new normal (and recovery isn't flagged as a change). Early in the mission, fall back to the last 14 green readings incl. pre-flight. Expect a few amber flags in flight days 1-14 as the body adapts (e.g. BP drops ~9 mmHg) - label this 'adaptation phase' in the UI.
